title: Android Kotlin Collection Processing
description: Beginner-to-advanced Kotlin collection reference for Android, covering mutability, transformations, filtering, grouping, aggregation, sequences, primitive arrays, persistent collections, allocation, complexity, concurrency boundaries, and production patterns.

sections.title: Collection Foundations
sections.description: Core collection types and naming rules.

subtopics.title: List, Set & Map
subtopics.description: The main Kotlin collection shapes and their mutable variants.

table.title: Kotlin Collection Selection
rows: By index; membership is generally linear
Membership is typically constant-time for hash sets
By key, typically constant-time for hash maps
A multi-step pipeline can avoid intermediate collections
One clear owner needs controlled mutation

tabs.label: Quick Reference
tabs.code:
val list = listOf(1, 2, 2)
val mutableList = mutableListOf(1, 2)

val set = setOf(1, 2, 2)
val mutableSet = mutableSetOf(1, 2)

val map = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2)
val mutableMap = mutableMapOf("a" to 1)

tabs.label: Detailed Example
tabs.code:
val names = mutableListOf("Alex", "Ben")
names += "Cara"
names.remove("Ben")

val roles = mutableSetOf("admin", "reader")
roles += "editor"

val scores = mutableMapOf("Alex" to 90)
scores["Ben"] = 85

annotations.text: Mutable collections expose add, remove, clear, and update operations.

callouts.text: List preserves order and duplicates; Set stores unique values; Map stores key-value pairs.
Read-only collections prevent mutation through that reference, but are not always deeply immutable.

codeBlocks.code:
By       → use a selector or key
Indexed  → lambda also receives the index
OrNull   → return null instead of throwing
Not      → invert the condition
Last     → work from the end
While    → continue until the condition becomes false

callouts.text: Think in stages: transform → filter → select → group → aggregate.

subtopics.title: Primitive Arrays & Persistent Immutable Collections
subtopics.description: Use primitive arrays only for measured numeric or binary hot paths; use persistent immutable collections when many versions share structure and ownership must be explicit.

tabs.label: Primitive Arrays
tabs.code:
val pixels: IntArray = IntArray(width * height)
val samples: FloatArray = floatArrayOf(0.1f, 0.4f, 0.9f)

// Avoid boxing from List<Int> in a measured numeric hot path.
val total = pixels.sumOf(Int::toLong)

tabs.label: Persistent Collections
tabs.code:
val initial: PersistentList<Item> = persistentListOf(a, b)
val next = initial.add(c)       // initial remains valid
val updated = next.set(0, a2)  // structure is shared internally

callouts.title: Different Trade-Offs
callouts.text: Primitive arrays reduce boxing but expose mutable indexed storage. Persistent collections provide immutable values with structural sharing but add a library and different performance characteristics. Measure realistic workloads.

Detailed Example
tabs.code:
data class Summary(val count: Int, val total: Double)

val summary = products.fold(Summary(0, 0.0)) { acc, product ->
    acc.copy(
        count = acc.count + 1,
        total = acc.total + product.price
    )
}

COMMON MISTAKES
❌ Using map only for side effects
❌ Putting forEach in the middle of a transformation chain
❌ Calling first() when no result may exist
❌ Confusing takeWhile with filter
❌ Ignoring duplicate-key replacement in associateBy
❌ Using Sequence for tiny, simple collections
❌ Mutating unrelated external state inside map or filter

QUICK REFERENCE

callouts.text: Prefer clear chains of small operations over one large lambda with several responsibilities.

sections.title: Mutability, Copying & Destinations
sections.description: Control ownership and allocation when collections cross Android architecture boundaries.

subtopics.title: Read-Only Is Not Deeply Immutable
subtopics.description: Kotlin's List, Set, and Map interfaces prevent mutation through that reference, but the backing collection or contained objects may still mutate.

codeBlocks.code:
val backing = mutableListOf("A")
val exposed: List<String> = backing
backing += "B" // exposed now also observes B

// Snapshot ownership at the boundary:
val snapshot: List<String> = backing.toList()

data class UiState(val users: List<User>)

callouts.title: Snapshot at Ownership Boundaries
callouts.text: When a repository or ViewModel publishes state, copy or use a persistent immutable collection if another owner could still mutate the backing data.

callouts.title: Shallow Copy
callouts.text: toList copies the container, not mutable elements. Prefer immutable element models or explicitly deep-copy where the domain requires isolation.

subtopics.title: +, -, += and Mutation
subtopics.description: plus/minus return new collections. += mutates a mutable receiver when plusAssign exists, but reassigns a read-only var using plus otherwise.

codeBlocks.code:
val original = listOf(1, 2)
val added = original + 3          // new List

val mutable = mutableListOf(1, 2)
mutable += 3                      // mutates MutableList

var readOnly: List<Int> = listOf(1, 2)
readOnly += 3                     // readOnly = readOnly + 3; allocates

callouts.title: Repeated + Can Be Quadratic
callouts.text: Building a large List with result = result + item copies the growing list on every iteration. Use buildList, a mutable builder, or a destination operator.

subtopics.title: mapTo, filterTo & Collection Builders
subtopics.description: Destination variants reuse or select a result collection type; buildList/buildMap expose controlled mutation only inside the builder.

tabs.label: Destination
Builder

callouts.title: Clarity Before Micro-Allocation
callouts.text: Use ordinary map/filter by default. Destination variants matter in measured hot paths, when appending to an existing result, or when the result type is semantically important.

sections.title: Advanced Grouping, Indexing & Duplicates
sections.description: Build indices and summaries without losing records accidentally.

subtopics.title: Duplicate Key Policies
subtopics.description: associateBy keeps the last value for a duplicate key. Choose reject, first, last, or group explicitly when duplicates carry meaning.

tabs.label: Reject
Group
tabs.code: val byEmail: Map<String, List<User>> = users.groupBy { it.email.lowercase() }

tabs.label: First Wins
tabs.code:
val firstById = users.fold(mutableMapOf<UserId, User>()) { acc, user ->
    acc.putIfAbsent(user.id, user)
    acc
}

callouts.title: Silent Overwrite Is Data Loss
callouts.text: If uniqueness is a domain invariant, validate it. Do not let associateBy silently hide malformed server or database data.

subtopics.title: groupingBy fold, reduce & aggregate
subtopics.description: Grouping operations calculate per-key results without allocating a List for every group as groupBy does.

codeBlocks.code:
data class Order(val customerId: CustomerId, val total: Long)

val spendByCustomer: Map<CustomerId, Long> = orders
    .groupingBy(Order::customerId)
    .fold(0L) { total, order -> total + order.total }

val counts = orders.groupingBy(Order::customerId).eachCount()

callouts.title: Use aggregate for Full Control
callouts.text: aggregate exposes key, current accumulator, element, and first-element status. Prefer fold/eachCount when they express the calculation more clearly.

sections.title: Complexity, Concurrency & Android UI
sections.description: Make performance and thread-safety choices based on actual collection size, access pattern, and ownership.

subtopics.title: Complexity & Allocation Guide
subtopics.description: Most transformations scan O(n) and allocate a result; sorting is O(n log n); repeated linear membership can turn a pipeline quadratic.

codeBlocks.code:
List index access: usually O(1)
List contains/remove by value: O(n)
Set/Map lookup: average O(1), subject to hashing
map/filter/distinct: O(n), allocate result structures
sorted/sortedBy: O(n log n), allocate/reorder references
groupBy: O(n) plus lists for every key
list.filter { it.id in selectedList }: O(n × m)
Convert selected IDs to Set first: O(n + m) average

callouts.title: Choose Structure Before Optimizing Lambdas
callouts.text: Replacing repeated List membership with a Set or prebuilt Map usually matters more than reducing a small lambda allocation. Profile realistic devices and data.

subtopics.title: Thread Safety & Publication
subtopics.description: Standard mutable collections are not thread-safe. Prefer single ownership and immutable snapshots across coroutine/thread boundaries.

callouts.title: Collections Do Not Become Safe Inside a Coroutine
callouts.text: Coroutines can run concurrently and resume on different threads. Use confinement, Mutex, actors, concurrent structures, or atomic immutable-state updates.

subtopics.title: Collections as Android UI State
subtopics.description: Publish immutable lists with stable item identity. Compute expensive projections outside rendering or memoize them against correct inputs.

callouts.title: New Container, New Changed Elements
callouts.text: Copy only changed immutable elements while reusing unchanged objects. Diffing and Compose skipping can then use stable identity/equality effectively.

callouts.title: Flow Is a Different Abstraction
callouts.text: Collection operators process in-memory elements; Flow operators process asynchronous emissions. See Android Kotlin Flows for cancellation, context, buffering, and sharing.

subtopics.title: Production Checklist
subtopics.description: Review semantics, ownership, absence, duplicates, allocation, complexity, and thread safety.

codeBlocks.code:
□ List/Set/Map matches ordering and uniqueness needs
□ Read-only references are not mistaken for deep immutability
□ Mutable backing data does not escape its owner
□ OrNull/empty behavior matches expected absence
□ Duplicate keys have an explicit policy
□ Side effects are not hidden inside map/filter
□ Repeated + is not used to build large collections
□ List membership in loops is replaced by Set/Map where useful
□ Sequence is used only for a measured/structural benefit
□ Sorting/grouping allocations are acceptable for input size
□ Shared mutable collections are confined or synchronized
□ UI lists use immutable values and stable IDs
